article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Zoo U: a single-player point-and-click game assessing six social skills in school-like scenes
description: Zoo U is a single-player point-and-click problem-solving game set in a school-like setting with teacher and student NPCs and zoo animals. Subject matter experts used educational and developmental psychology theories to develop six independent social scenes assessing "emotion regulation, impulse control, communication, empathy, cooperation, and initiation." Each scene scores a composite performance index computed from parsed log files, combining dialogue-choice quality, time spent on appropriate versus off-task problem solving, and the ratio of on-task to off-task behaviors.
requirements: Scene content developed by subject matter experts to elicit measurable player behaviors and dialogue choices integral to the assessed social skill
Computer logs tracking the location and time of each mouse click
constraints: Students' scores decline if they diverge too far from on-task behavior; each scene varies in emphasis on NPC interaction versus environment interaction
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade students in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: assessment of children's social skills aptitude across six social competencies
examples: In the impulse control scene, players must ignore red-herring food crates and read the clipboard feeding instructions to score highly
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: The critical, relational practice of instructional design in higher education: an emerging model of change agency
citation: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007).
title: Zone of moral coherence as the alignment condition for agentic instructional design practice
description: The article contends instructional design should be understood as a moral practice and proposes a zone of moral coherence: when the values of designers, clients, institutions and the profession align, agency operates coherently and with greater impact. "In cases where there is agreement among agencies concerning the values, ethical and functional dimensions of agency, we suggest that the overall agency is operating in a zone of moral coherence." Where agencies conflict, the effect of agency is tempered and potentially negated, producing dissonance that may lead designers to question staying in the profession.
requirements: Alignment among the values of designers, clients, organizations and learners
constraints: Designers are at times required to practice outside the zone, causing moral incoherence and dissonance
target_learning_goals: navigating value conflicts in design work
examples: A designer left a position after repeated contradictory supervisor instructions in a rigid, cookie-cutter environment, illustrating moral incoherence
key_sources: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9061-6

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: ZAA and ZPA as constructs relating the ZPD to educational technology
description: The article defines two constructs that clarify the relationship between the ZPD and educational technology. "The ZAA is used to describe the types of resources, both human and artifact, that are available within a particular context"; the ZPA is "a selected subset of the ZAA that are the resources that are the most appropriate form of assistance for a given learner at a particular moment in time". The article stresses that a rich ZAA alone does not create a ZPD: a more able partner must organise and activate resources, or make existing assistance obvious, so the learner can select appropriately.
requirements: A more able partner must organise and activate the available resources appropriately for the learner to form a ZPA
constraints: The existence of a rich set of resources within the ZAA is not sufficient to ensure the interactions necessary to create a ZPD
target_learners: learners working with more able partners, including teachers, parents and software
target_learning_goals: receiving appropriately challenging activities with the right quantity and quality of assistance
examples: In earlier software scaffolding work the ZAA was within the software, with scaffolding techniques making timely interventions to draw the learner's attention to available assistance, thus creating a ZPA
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.09.018

article_title: Recommendations for the Investigation and Delivery of Music Programs Aimed at Achieving Psychosocial Wellbeing Benefits in Mainstream Schools
citation: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://www.asme.edu.au/
title: Two dominant assumptions — that generic music education programs achieve PSWB benefits and that standard quantitative self-report methods can capture them — are unwarranted 'zombie categories'
description: The article identifies two assumptions dominating research and policy: that generic music education programs will facilitate student PSWB, and that quantitative self-report methods are suitable for capturing PSWB benefits. Drawing on critical theory and borrowing from Beck (2002) and Plummer (2011), the authors call these "'zombie categories'" — approaches that are unhelpful in this area and that obscure the reality research aims to uncover, potentially threatening policy support for school music programs.
requirements: Research and policy in this area must be re-designed to avoid relying on these two assumptions when claiming or evaluating PSWB benefits
constraints: The article states its recommendations do not account for all potential challenges nor sufficiently address all those identified
examples: The two studies reported here both used pre-post survey designs dominating the field, and both returned null survey results while interviews reported benefits
key_sources: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061963

article_title: The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives
citation: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18
title: Zodiac-sign authentic reading texts with dictionary lookup and personal description writing
description: The instructional material evaluated in the study: 12 short printed texts about the 12 zodiac signs, one per session, treated as authentic materials because "everybody has his or her own sign according to their birth month". Learners read each text, looked unknown adjectives up in their dictionaries, and wrote a short description of a classmate or family member born under the same sign using the learned adjectives. The control group instead received dictionary extracts of the same adjectives.
requirements: Target adjectives must be unknown to learners beforehand; known words were omitted from treatment and post-test
constraints: Content is tied to learners' birth months and zodiac signs, a specific authenticity framing
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners in intact classes
examples: The vocabulary post-test comprised 42 multiple-choice items that were completely unknown to the learners after the pre-test screening
key_sources: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18

article_title: Simultaneous Remote Laparoscopic Training for Trainees Among Multiple Institutions: Can Remote Coaching Replace On-Site Coaching?
citation: Baba Kenji, Hozaka Yuto, Tanabe Kan, Wada Masumi, Kuroshima Naoki, Takara Kinjo, Yoshidome Shizuka, Iio Shunya, Okubo Keishi, Uenosono Yoshikazu, Shimonosono Masakata, Kawasaki Yota, Sasaki Ken, Arigami Takaaki, Ohtsuka Takao. (2024). Simultaneous Remote Laparoscopic Training for Trainees Among Multiple Institutions: Can Remote Coaching Replace On‐Site Coaching? Asian Journal of Endoscopic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1111/ases.70007
title: Simultaneous multi-institution Zoom-based laparoscopic training curriculum with training boxes and real-time remote coaching
description: A three-session curriculum of lectures, practical training, and assessments delivered 1 hour per week, connecting a university hospital and three rural hospitals via Zoom. The article states "all sites were connected via Zoom … for real‐time interactive sessions", with a supervising surgeon giving 15-min lectures and monitoring 30-min practice via an iPad and training box at each facility. A maximum of six trainees trained simultaneously, with no more than two per facility.
requirements: Standard Wi-Fi internet connection at each facility
A training box, an iPad, and laparoscopic instruments and consumable supplies at each facility
At least one senior surgeon present at each facility in case of unexpected situations
constraints: A maximum of six trainees were trained simultaneously, with no more than two participants from each facility
Time available to supervise each participant was limited because multiple facilities trained simultaneously
target_learners: Postgraduate year 1–5 surgical trainees at university and rural hospitals
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic suture ligation skills, including knot tying and advanced techniques such as overwrapping and running sutures
examples: The first session introduced essential tools and hand-eye coordination, the second covered square, slip, and surgeon's knots, and the third covered overwrapping, wrapping, and running sutures

(2024). Simultaneous Remote Laparoscopic Training for Trainees Among Multiple Institutions: Can Remote Coaching Replace On‐Site Coaching? Asian Journal of Endoscopic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1111/ases.70007

article_title: Measuring Students' Use of Zoom Application in Language Course Based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM).
citation: Alfadda, Hind Abdulaziz, & Mahdi, Hassan Saleh. (2021). Measuring Students’ Use of Zoom Application in Language Course Based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-020-09752-1
title: Zoom web conference system as a synchronous language-learning environment
description: Zoom is a subscription-based web conferencing program that supports synchronous interaction between educators and students via webcam and microphone in real time. The article describes its educational activities: "communication-related activities include greeting others, classroom lectures, question and answers and group discussions in breakout rooms", plus material-sharing, polling, whiteboard practice, and recordable individual meetings. In this study it mediated the emergency shift to at-home EFL learning for 75 Saudi undergraduates during COVID-19 university closures.
requirements: Reliable internet connection, adequate speakers or microphones, and a quiet environment for students to participate effectively
constraints: The article notes Zoom features may be difficult to access at first and less intuitive, students may become distracted or multitask, and free accounts historically limited sessions to 40 minutes
target_learning_goals: synchronous communication, lectures, group discussion and practice activities in language courses
examples: Students in the study used Zoom alongside BlackBoard in the 2019/2020 academic year affected by COVID-19 closures
key_sources: Alfadda, Hind Abdulaziz, & Mahdi, Hassan Saleh. (2021). Measuring Students’ Use of Zoom Application in Language Course Based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-020-09752-1

article_title: Authentic Research in the Classroom for Teachers and Students
citation: L. M. Rebull. (2018). Authentic Research in the Classroom for Teachers and Students. https://nitarp.ipac.caltech.edu
title: Zooniverse and Disk Detective as citizen science entry points
description: Zooniverse is a citizen science platform with many astronomy projects to choose from, positioned at the widest part of the funnel. Lesson plans provide a framework for canned use of the data, supporting educators just getting started. One project, Disk Detective, places the RA and Dec of each object with a link to SIMBAD on object pages, and used Zooniverse to find the few most highly interested and capable amateurs worldwide, who now join weekly science meetings. The author notes "Citizen Science at its best enables “hooks” for interested people to go further".
requirements: Participation requires no deep understanding of astrophysics or programming
constraints: Citizen science is generally removed from the scientific process, which is messier than simplified interfaces permit; intensive engagement down the funnel is not something all Zooniverse projects do
target_learners: young children through senior citizens worldwide
target_learning_goals: contributing small pieces to real science that can result in refereed journal articles
examples: Disk Detective's inner circle of dedicated volunteers participates in getting new data and attends weekly science meetings
key_sources: L. M. Rebull. (2018). Authentic Research in the Classroom for Teachers and Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.08747

article_title: Harnessing Transparent Learning Analytics for Individualized Support through Auto-detection of Engagement in Face-to-Face Collaborative Learning
citation: Qi Zhou, Wannapon Suraworachet, and Mutlu Cukurova. 2024. Harnessing Transparent Learning Analytics for Individualized Support through Auto-detection of Engagement in Face-to-Face Collaborative Learning. In The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24). https://doi.org/10.1145/3636555.3636894
title: Zoom Lens multilevel collaboration analytics framework
description: The Zoom Lens framework is a multilevel collaboration analytics framework proposed by Zhou and Cukurova as an extension of the 'from clicks to constructs' framework. It “extended the human-observable behaviours of the previous framework into three different types of behaviours, namely social signals, group interactions and individual engagement”. Group interactions are detected from each individual's social signals, while individual engagement is estimated based on that social signal and the group interaction happening. This study applies Zoom Lens and operationalises it with a rule-based automatic detection of individual engagement from group interactions.
requirements: Requires detection of individual behaviours (gaze and speech) from which group interactions are inferred, and estimation of individual engagement from both individual behaviours and the corresponding group interaction
constraints: The article focuses only on two of the levels at which transparency can be damaged: the transparency of the models and the level of analysis for an individual learner
target_learners: postgraduate students in face-to-face collaborative learning
examples: Applied in a 10-week postgraduate module where students collaborated on an educational technology design case in weekly two-hour face-to-face sessions
key_sources: Qi Zhou, Wannapon Suraworachet, and Mutlu Cukurova. 2024. Harnessing Transparent Learning Analytics for Individualized Support through Auto-detection of Engagement in Face-to-Face Collaborative Learning. In The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24). https://doi.org/10.1145/3636555.3636894

article_title: Semantic-Driven Topic Modeling for Analyzing Creativity in Virtual Brainstorming
citation: Melkamu Abay Mersha, Jugal Kalita. (2026). Semantic-Driven Topic Modeling for Analyzing Creativity in Virtual Brainstorming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16835
title: Zoom brainstorming transcript dataset from student groups improving their university
description: A transcript corpus collected through collaborative brainstorming sessions in virtual meetings with "three to five participants in each group", conducted via Zoom videoconferencing. Each group held a 60-minute session generating ideas on ways to improve their university; participants were graduate and undergraduate students of various majors at a US university. The resulting text data served as the evaluation dataset for the framework and its baselines.
requirements: Structured brainstorming prompts and Zoom transcript capture
target_learning_goals: collaborative ideation and group creativity assessment
examples: Groups were instructed to generate ideas on ways to improve their university
key_sources: Melkamu Abay Mersha, Jugal Kalita. (2026). Semantic-Driven Topic Modeling for Analyzing Creativity in Virtual Brainstorming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16835

article_title: How often does unguided peer interaction lead to correct response consensus? An example from Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism
citation: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2024). How often does unguided peer interaction lead to correct response consensus? An example from Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism.
title: Zone of proximal facilitation (ZPF) model of collaborative learning
description: The ZPF model, building on Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, is the framework the article uses to predict when unguided peer collaboration succeeds. "This model predicts the success of collaborative learning when students have some knowledge in the area, but they cannot complete the task on their own." If a task is within the group's ZPF, adequate group competence can yield successful outcomes; if beyond it, students may not benefit. For a pair, the task can be in the ZPD of the group but out of each student's individual ZPD.
requirements: Students must have some knowledge in the area
The task must lie within the group's zone of proximal facilitation
constraints: If the task is beyond the competence of the group defined by the ZPF, students may not benefit from peer collaboration
target_learners: student pairs and groups collaborating without instructor guidance
target_learning_goals: solving problems students cannot solve individually by leveraging collective expertise
examples: The authors interpret Q30's negative shift and Q14's incorrect consensus as cases where difficulty exceeded a particular group's ZPF
key_sources: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2024). How often does unguided peer interaction lead to correct response consensus? An example from Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13806

article_title: Using Unguided Peer Collaboration to Facilitate Early Educators' Pedagogical Development: An Example from Physics TA Training
citation: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2025). Using Unguided Peer Collaboration to Facilitate Early Educators' Pedagogical Development: An Example from Physics TA Training. https://www.physport.org
title: Zone of Proximal Facilitation (ZPF) model
description: The Zone of Proximal Facilitation model builds on Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development and is used in this article to explain why unguided peer collaboration improves performance. The article states it "predict[s] that students with some knowledge of the content but unable to complete tasks individually can succeed through collaboration and learn, leveraging their collective expertise." The authors apply it to interpret TAs' high construction and co-construction rates, concluding that most MCS items came under the zone of proximal facilitation of the group. It is paired in the article with distributed cognition as a framework supporting collaborative work.
requirements: Peers must have some knowledge of the content so their collective expertise can be leveraged during collaboration
constraints: The article frames the model as a prediction framework rather than testing it directly
target_learners: college and high school introductory physics students
examples: The authors interpret that most MCS items came under the zone of proximal facilitation of the group given the high construction and co-construction rates
key_sources: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2025). Using Unguided Peer Collaboration to Facilitate Early Educators' Pedagogical Development: An Example from Physics TA Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14046

article_title: Virtual high voltage lab: gamified learning in a safe 3d environment
citation: Pliuhin, V., Tsegelnyk, Y., Sukhonos, M., Biletskyi, I., Plankovskyy, S., and Sakhoshko, T. (2024). Virtual High Voltage Lab: Gamified Learning in a Safe 3D Environment. O.M. Beketov National University of Urban Economy in Kharkiv.
title: Zoned virtual-lab layout separating instruction, interaction, and recovery
description: VLab-HV organizes the virtual space into functional zones that serve different pedagogical roles. "A lecture zone displays safety posters detailing international standards, such as IEC 60060-1, providing critical information on HV safety protocols and reinforcing theoretical knowledge." "A recreation zone, adorned with calming decor such as plants and ambient lighting, mitigates cognitive overload during extended sessions." Interactive elements (vending machine quizzes, AI robots, a virtual drone for inspection, a transformable Optimus Prime toy referencing transformers) sit between these poles, structuring engagement and rest within one environment.
requirements: Distinct spatial zones with distinct content roles; interactive objects that dispense prompts or guidance; calming decor in rest areas
constraints: The article describes the layout as design intent; no comparative evaluation of the zoning is printed in the supplied text
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in virtual laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement, cognitive-load management, safety knowledge reinforcement
examples: A virtual vending machine dispenses quizzes on HV fundamentals or safety protocols, rewarding correct answers with points; a virtual drone enables multi-perspective equipment inspection
key_sources: Pliuhin, V., Tsegelnyk, Y., Sukhonos, M., Biletskyi, I., Plankovskyy, S., and Sakhoshko, T. (2024). Virtual High Voltage Lab: Gamified Learning in a Safe 3D Environment. O.M. Beketov National University of Urban Economy in Kharkiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20919

citation: Carlson Eric R. DMD, MD, EdM. (2020). COVID-19 and Educational Engagement. Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joms.2020.04.033
title: Zoom videoconferencing as a platform for maintaining engagement in OMS education during COVID-19
description: Zoom Meetings is described as "a solution to maintaining engagement in OMS education" during the pandemic, supporting physical distancing while maintaining relative social contact. The system "enumerates participants in the meeting and enables collective or individual interactive typed chat discussions, muting of distracting background noise, sharing of documents, and selection of custom backgrounds." The article reports Zoom use increased 67% during the first 3 months of 2020 owing to the pandemic, reaching 40 million users of Zoom Meetings with 65,000 subscribed organizations.
requirements: Educators should ensure residents use video cameras during Zoom sessions to permit relative social contact
constraints: The objective of Zoom technology is not to create the essential element of emotion in the engagement process but rather to leverage that emotion
target_learning_goals: maintaining educational engagement during remote instruction
examples: The author's stated experience is that Socratic teaching can occur with combined video and audio conferencing during the COVID-19 pandemic
key_sources: Carlson Eric R. DMD, MD, EdM. (2020). COVID-19 and Educational Engagement. Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joms.2020.04.033
